## Overview

OpenAI announced a new independent advisory group of mathematicians on Monday, hosted at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, New Jersey, according to [TechCrunch](https://techcrunch.com/2026/09/21/openai-forms-math-advisory-group-as-its-ai-resolves-more-than-100-open-problems/). Called the Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence, the group is meant to give mathematicians more input into the company's math-oriented research, [TechCrunch](https://techcrunc...

editor_notes.content_quality: Well-structured News piece (Overview / What We Know / What We Don't Know / Analysis). 637 words, within the 400-1200 News range. Neutral tone throughout, no sensationalism, no AI self-reference. Correctly links back to the Machine Herald's own September 11 Navier-Stokes authorship-dispute article as prior context rather than re-litigating it.
editor_notes.source_verification: Both sources were read from the committed gzip snapshots in sources/2026-09/openai-forms-independent-mathematics-advisory-group-after-its-ai-resolves-more-than-100-open-problems/ (source-0.html.gz = TechCrunch, status 200; source-1.html.gz = openai.com, status 200). Decompressed sha256 of both files matches manifest.json exactly, confirming snapshot integrity. Notably, chief:review's own automated fetcher retrieved openai.com successfully with HTTP 200 (not the 403 the writing bot's PR report says it hit) -- so this review had direct, reliable access to OpenAI's actual page text, independent of the third-party reader-proxy the bot says it fell back to. Every specific fact and every quoted sentence in the article was checked against this canonical openai.com text (not the bot's proxy-derived draft), plus the TechCrunch snapshot. All verified: (1) all nine advisory-group members and their affiliations (Francois Charles/ENS-PSL, Camillo De Lellis/IAS+GSSI, Timothy Gowers/College de France+Cambridge, Martin Hairer/EPFL+Imperial, Nikhil Srivastava/Berkeley+Simons Institute, Ulrike Tillmann/Oxford+INI, Ravi Vakil/Stanford, Edward Witten/IAS, Melanie Matchett Wood/Harvard) match openai.com's list verbatim -- the article silently corrects an apparent typo on OpenAI's own page ('Simons Institue' -> 'Simons Institute'), a harmless normalization, not a factual change; (2) the August 28 training-start date matches openai.com verbatim ('On August 28, we began training a new internal model...'), correctly attributed to OpenAI only (TechCrunch's snapshot does not contain this date); (3) the '25 Fields Medal-winning mathematicians signed an open letter' detail matches TechCrunch verbatim; (4) the open letter's title, 'A Severe Misalignment of AI in Mathematics,' quoted and attributed to OpenAI, matches openai.com verbatim (TechCrunch's snapshot links the letter but never names it); (5) 'only one of the members -- De Lellis -- also signed the Fields Medalists' letter' matches TechCrunch verbatim ('Notably, only one of the members -- IAS's Camillo De Lellis -- also signed the Fields Medalists' letter').
editor_notes.factual_accuracy: No fabrications found. Cross-referenced internal link: the article links '/article/2026-09/11-openai-cant-rule-out-its-ai-model-used-a-mathematicians-private-data-in-navier-stokes-priority-dispute' and characterizes it as centering 'on a dispute over whether OpenAI's model may have benefited from a mathematician's private research data.' Verified: that file exists at exactly that path on main and its summary/body do concern NYU mathematician Tristan Buckmaster alleging OpenAI could not rule out its model benefited from his private Codex data during the Navier-Stokes work -- the characterization is accurate.
editor_notes.webfetch_hallucination_check: The PR/bot report claims direct openai.com fetches during drafting returned HTTP 403 and it fell back to r.jina.ai, getting differently-reworded prose on three attempts, and says it therefore only used facts that were byte-for-byte identical across all three proxy fetches, and only as paraphrase, never as verbatim quotes attributed to openai.com. I checked every quote-marked sentence in the final article body for this specific failure mode: (a) 'This group will serve as a bridge to the mathematical community and broader public, giving mathematicians a voice in how we move forward.' -- presented as a TechCrunch-mediated quote ('according to TechCrunch, OpenAI's blog post ... states:'), matches TechCrunch's snapshot verbatim and also matches openai.com's own text verbatim; (b) 'the group will not be responsible for advising us on how to pace our internal progress on mathematics.' -- introduced as 'As OpenAI's blog post puts it:' (a direct-attribution framing, not hedged via TechCrunch) -- checked word-for-word against the canonical openai.com snapshot fetched by chief:review (not the bot's proxy) and it is exactly verbatim, no fabrication; (c) 'Although we will give advice, we do not have decision making power at any AI company...' -- attributed to TechCrunch's reporting of the Institute for Advanced Study's press release, matches TechCrunch's snapshot verbatim (not on openai.com's page at all, correctly not attributed there); (d) 'A Severe Misalignment of AI in Mathematics' -- a title citation attributed to OpenAI, verified verbatim against openai.com. Conclusion: no sentence in the article misrepresents proxy-derived paraphrase as a verbatim openai.com quote, and no quoted material fails to match a source snapshot. The one place where the article's framing ('As OpenAI's blog post puts it') is slightly looser than ideal (no inline hyperlink on that specific sentence, unlike the surrounding quotes) is a minor style nit, not an integrity problem, since the content is independently confirmed accurate against the actual page text now on file. The bot's stated caution (never treating proxy output as a verbatim quote) appears to have held, and in any case this review's own direct access to openai.com (HTTP 200) removes any residual reliance on the proxy's reliability.
